claim: The glymphatic system is a brain-wide clearance pathway.
source: The glymphatic system is a brain-wide clearance pathway; its impairment contributes to the accumulation of amyloid-β.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about the glymphatic system.

claim: Impairment of the glymphatic system contributes to the accumulation of amyloid-β.
source: The glymphatic system is a brain-wide clearance pathway; its impairment contributes to the accumulation of amyloid-β.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Influx of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) depends upon the expression and perivascular localization of the astroglial water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4).
source: Influx of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) depends upon the expression and perivascular localization of the astroglial water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4).
evidence: This is a central claim of the manuscript stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout.

claim: CSF influx is higher in wild-type mice than in four different Aqp4 KO lines.
source: We concur that CSF influx is higher in wild-type mice than in four different Aqp4 KO lines and in one line that lacks perivascular AQP4 (Snta1 KO).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from five independent laboratories presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: CSF influx is higher in wild-type mice than in Snta1 KO mice that lack perivascular AQP4.
source: We concur that CSF influx is higher in wild-type mice than in four different Aqp4 KO lines and in one line that lacks perivascular AQP4 (Snta1 KO).
evidence: This claim is supported by DCE-MRI data from the OHSU group presented in Figure 6.

claim: Meta-analysis of all studies demonstrated a significant decrease in tracer transport in KO mice and rats compared to controls.
source: Meta-analysis of all studies demonstrated a significant decrease in tracer transport in KO mice and rats compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results presented in Figure 8.

claim: Anesthesia, age, and tracer delivery explain the opposing results between studies.
source: Meta-regression indicated that anesthesia, age, and tracer delivery explain the opposing results.
evidence: This claim is based on meta-regression analysis of the compiled studies.

claim: Intrastriatal injections suppress glymphatic function.
source: We also report that intrastriatal injections suppress glymphatic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Glymphatic studies must avoid the use of invasive procedures.
source: This validates the role of AQP4 and shows that glymphatic studies must avoid the use of invasive procedures.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings showing that invasive procedures suppress CSF influx.

claim: The glymphatic system supports the rapid exchange of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and interstitial fluid (ISF) along perivascular pathways.
source: A brain-wide fluid transport pathway, known as the glymphatic system, supports the rapid exchange of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and interstitial fluid (ISF) along perivascular pathways (Iliff et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: The glymphatic system consists of CSF inflow along perivascular spaces surrounding penetrating arteries.
source: The glymphatic system consists of three principal sequential anatomic segments: (i) CSF inflow along the perivascular spaces surrounding penetrating arteries, (ii) dispersion of CSF through the wider interstitium, and (iii) efflux of ISF along the large-caliber draining veins to re-enter the CSF within the ventricular and cisternal compartments (Jessen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the anatomical structure of the glymphatic system as cited from previous work.

claim: The glymphatic system includes dispersion of CSF through the wider interstitium.
source: The glymphatic system consists of three principal sequential anatomic segments: (i) CSF inflow along the perivascular spaces surrounding penetrating arteries, (ii) dispersion of CSF through the wider interstitium, and (iii) efflux of ISF along the large-caliber draining veins to re-enter the CSF within the ventricular and cisternal compartments (Jessen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the anatomical structure of the glymphatic system as cited from previous work.

claim: The glymphatic system includes efflux of ISF along large-caliber draining veins to re-enter the CSF within the ventricular and cisternal compartments.
source: The glymphatic system consists of three principal sequential anatomic segments: (i) CSF inflow along the perivascular spaces surrounding penetrating arteries, (ii) dispersion of CSF through the wider interstitium, and (iii) efflux of ISF along the large-caliber draining veins to re-enter the CSF within the ventricular and cisternal compartments (Jessen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the anatomical structure of the glymphatic system as cited from previous work.

claim: Interstitial solutes cleared to the CSF exit the brain through meningeal lymphatic vessels flanking the venous sinuses.
source: Ultimately, interstitial solutes cleared to the CSF exit the brain through meningeal lymphatic vessels flanking the venous sinuses, along cranial and spinal nerve sheathes, and across the cribriform plate (Louveau et al., 2015; Aspelund et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim describes CSF drainage pathways and is supported by citations.

claim: Interstitial solutes cleared to the CSF exit the brain along cranial and spinal nerve sheathes.
source: Ultimately, interstitial solutes cleared to the CSF exit the brain through meningeal lymphatic vessels flanking the venous sinuses, along cranial and spinal nerve sheathes, and across the cribriform plate (Louveau et al., 2015; Aspelund et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim describes CSF drainage pathways and is supported by citations.

claim: Interstitial solutes cleared to the CSF exit the brain across the cribriform plate.
source: Ultimately, interstitial solutes cleared to the CSF exit the brain through meningeal lymphatic vessels flanking the venous sinuses, along cranial and spinal nerve sheathes, and across the cribriform plate (Louveau et al., 2015; Aspelund et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim describes CSF drainage pathways and is supported by citations.

claim: Astrocytic endfeet ensheath the cerebral vasculature.
source: Astrocytic endfeet ensheath the cerebral vasculature, and the abundantly expressed astroglial water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4) localizes primarily to the perivascular endfoot membrane domain abutting the basal lamina.
evidence: This is an anatomical description supported by established knowledge.

claim: AQP4 localizes primarily to the perivascular endfoot membrane domain abutting the basal lamina.
source: Astrocytic endfeet ensheath the cerebral vasculature, and the abundantly expressed astroglial water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4) localizes primarily to the perivascular endfoot membrane domain abutting the basal lamina.
evidence: This is an anatomical description supported by established knowledge.

claim: AQP4 has been proposed to support perivascular fluid and solute movement along the glymphatic system.
source: As this anatomic arrangement provides a route for rapid water movement between the perivascular space and the glial syncytium, AQP4 has been proposed to support perivascular fluid and solute movement along the glymphatic system (Nedergaard, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Iliff et al. demonstrated a significant suppression of both perivascular CSF tracer influx and interstitial mannitol and amyloid-β clearance in Aqp4 knockout mice.
source: Iliff et al. demonstrated a significant suppression of both perivascular CSF tracer influx and interstitial mannitol and amyloid-β (Aβ) clearance in Aqp4 knockout (KO) mice (Iliff et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Aqp4 gene deletion exacerbated glymphatic pathway dysfunction after traumatic brain injury.
source: Subsequent work demonstrated that Aqp4 gene deletion exacerbated glymphatic pathway dysfunction after traumatic brain injury (TBI) and promoted the development of neurofibrillary pathology and neurodegeneration in the post-traumatic brain (Iliff et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Aqp4 gene deletion promoted the development of neurofibrillary pathology and neurodegeneration in the post-traumatic brain.
source: Subsequent work demonstrated that Aqp4 gene deletion exacerbated glymphatic pathway dysfunction after traumatic brain injury (TBI) and promoted the development of neurofibrillary pathology and neurodegeneration in the post-traumatic brain (Iliff et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Aqp4 KO mice exhibit slowed transport of interstitial solutes to the blood after TBI.
source: Plog et al. similarly found that Aqp4 KO mice exhibit slowed transport of interstitial solutes to the blood after TBI, reflected by a significant reduction in plasma biomarkers of TBI, including GFAP, neuron-specific enolase, and S100β (Plog et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Deletion of Aqp4 exacerbated Aβ plaque accumulation and cerebral amyloid angiopathy in the APP/PS1 murine model of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Xu et al. reported that deletion of Aqp4 exacerbated Aβ plaque accumulation and cerebral amyloid angiopathy in the APP/PS1 murine model of Alzheimer's disease (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Achariyar et al. found significantly reduced distribution of FITC-ApoE3, 125I-apoE2, 125I-apoE3, 125I-apoE4, and 14C-inulin in Aqp4 KO mice following tracer injection to the CSF.
source: Achariyar et al. found significantly reduced distribution of FITC-ApoE3, 125I-apoE2, 125I-apoE3, 125I-apoE4, as well as 14C-inulin in Aqp4 KO mice following tracer injection to the CSF (Achariyar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Glymphatic clearance of lactate was reduced in Aqp4 KO mice.
source: Lundgaard et al. reported that glymphatic clearance of lactate was reduced in Aqp4 KO mice (Lundgaard, 2016).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Aqp4 KO mice exhibit significantly impaired clearance of adeno-associated viruses (AAV) infused into the ventricles.
source: Finally, Murlidharan et al. demonstrated that Aqp4 KO mice exhibit significantly impaired clearance of adeno-associated viruses (AAV) infused into the ventricles, and concluded that glymphatic transport profoundly affects various aspects of AAV gene transfer in the CNS (Murlidharan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: The AQP4 facilitator TGN-073 potentiated the transport of interstitial fluid from the glia limitans externa to pericapillary Virchow-Robin space.
source: A recent MRI study showed the AQP4 facilitator, TGN-073, potentiated the transport of interstitial fluid from the glia limitans externa to pericapillary Virchow-Robin space (Huber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Smith et al. (2017) failed to detect any reduction in CSF tracer influx into the brain parenchyma of Aqp4 KO mice compared to wild-type controls.
source: The critical role of AQP4 in supporting perivascular CSF-ISF exchange was recently questioned in a report by Smith et al. (2017), in which the authors failed to detect any reduction in CSF tracer influx into the brain parenchyma of Aqp4 KO mice compared to wild-type (WT) controls.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study that contradicts the main hypothesis.

claim: Four independently generated Aqp4 KO lines were used in this study.
source: Our conclusion is strengthened by the use of four independently generated Aqp4 KO lines, including the line used by Smith et al. (2017), as well as the α-syntrophin (Snta1) KO line, which lacks AQP4 perivascular localization despite normal expression levels (Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the experimental design.

claim: The Snta1 KO line lacks AQP4 perivascular localization despite normal expression levels.
source: Our conclusion is strengthened by the use of four independently generated Aqp4 KO lines, including the line used by Smith et al. (2017), as well as the α-syntrophin (Snta1) KO line, which lacks AQP4 perivascular localization despite normal expression levels (Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a characterization of the Snta1 KO mouse line supported by citation.

claim: Traumatic brain injury is linked to an immediate and sustained reduction in CSF influx.
source: We questioned this approach based on the prior finding that traumatic brain injury is linked to an immediated and sustained reduction in CSF influx (Iliff et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on a cited previous finding.

claim: Insertion of glass pipettes into the brain markedly reduced brain-wide CSF tracer influx.
source: As expected, our analysis showed that insertion of glass pipettes into the brain markedly reduced brain-wide CSF tracer influx.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: AQP4 was deleted in all the Aqp4 KO mouse lines used in this study.
source: Immunohistochemistry done in parallel with the glymphatic experiments verified that AQP4 was indeed deleted in all the Aqp4 KO mouse lines (Figure 1a–c and e).
evidence: This claim is verified by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Perivascular AQP4 polarization was absent in Snta1 KO mice.
source: In the Snta1 KO mice, immunofluorescence demonstrated that perivascular AQP4 polarization was absent in this line (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is verified by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The mean integrated optical density (MIOD) of TRd3 on the dorsal and ventral brain surface was significantly reduced in Aqp4 KO mice compared with WT mice.
source: Quantification of the mean integrated optical density (MIOD) of TRd3 on the dorsal and ventral brain surface along anterior-posterior position of bregma showed a significant reduction in Aqp4 KO mice compared with WT mice (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the NMU group shown in Figure 2.

claim: CSF tracer entry into the ventral brain was higher than into the dorsal brain.
source: Interestingly, CSF tracer entry into the ventral brain was higher than into the dorsal brain.
evidence: This is an observation from the NMU experiments.

claim: The percentage area of whole-slice fluorescence was significantly reduced in Aqp4 KO mice compared to WT controls.
source: The percentage area of whole-slice fluorescence was significantly reduced in Aqp4 KO mice compared to WT controls (Figure 2d,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the NMU group shown in Figure 2.

claim: Penetration of CSF tracer was high in the ventral and lateral brain surface of WT mice.
source: Subregional quantification on the coronal section at the level of 0.5 mm anterior to the bregma showed that penetration of CSF tracer was high in the ventral and lateral brain surface of WT mice, but was comparable in the dorsal surface of the brain with Aqp4 KO mice (Figure 2g–h), further supporting difference in brain regions of CSF tracer influx.
evidence: This claim is supported by subregional analysis data from the NMU group shown in Figure 2.

claim: Aqp4 KO markedly impaired the influx of TR-d3 into both the perivascular space and the brain parenchyma in the hypothalamus.
source: Specifically, Aqp4 KO markedly impaired the influx of TR-d3 into both the perivascular space and the brain parenchyma in the hypothalamus, one of the brain regions with the highest expression of AQP4 (Fan et al., 2005; Nielsen et al., 1997) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the NMU group shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The tracer was almost undetectable at 500 µm below the brain surface in both the perivascular space and in the brain parenchyma in Aqp4 KO mice.
source: The tracer was almost undetectable at 500 µm below the brain surface in both the perivascular space and in the brain parenchyma in Aqp4 KO mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the NMU experiments.

claim: The TR-d3 fluorescence intensity remained at 90% of the pial surface intensity to a depth of 500 µm in the perivascular space as well as in the adjacent parenchyma in WT mice.
source: By contrast, the TR-d3 fluorescence intensity remained at 90% of the pial surface intensity to a depth of 500 µm in the perivascular space as well as in the adjacent parenchyma in WT mice (Figure 2i–j).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the NMU experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: BDA distribution appeared less extensive in the cortex of Aqp4 KO mice.
source: As a result, BDA distribution appeared less extensive in the cortex of Aqp4 KO mice (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is an observation from the RIKEN experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: BDA signals in the cortex of Aqp4 KO mice are of lower intensity and penetrated less into the parenchyma at an anterior-posterior position of bregma.
source: Notably, BDA signals in the cortex of Aqp4 KO mice are of lower intensity and penetrated less into the parenchyma at an anterior-posterior position of bregma (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the RIKEN group shown in Figure 3.

claim: BDA distribution in Aqp4 KO cortex is broadly compromised across the anterior-posterior extent of the cortex.
source: Indeed, Figure 3d shows that BDA distribution in Aqp4 KO cortex is broadly compromised.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the RIKEN group shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Parenchymal distribution of tracer showed a significant reduction in Aqp4 KO mice compared with both CD1 mice (Aqp4+/+) and wild-type C57BL/6 (WT) mice.
source: Parenchymal distribution of tracer showed a significant reduction in Aqp4 KO mice compared with both CD1 mice (Aqp4+/+) and wild-type C57BL/6 (WT) mice (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the UNC group shown in Figure 4.

claim: No significant difference in global tracer influx was seen between the two control groups (CD1 and C57BL/6).
source: No significant difference in global tracer influx was seen between the two control groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the UNC experiments comparing control strains.

claim: Differences in CSF influx between Aqp4 KO and controls was most notable in coronal sections anterior to bregma.
source: Differences in CSF influx between Aqp4 KO and controls was most notable in coronal sections anterior to bregma (Figure 4d), perhaps reflecting that these sections include the cortical segment of the middle cerebral artery, a main site of CSF influx.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the UNC group shown in Figure 4d and includes an interpretation.

claim: The difference in CSF influx was the result of decreased tracer penetration in the hypothalamus and areas of the basal forebrain.
source: Regional quantification showed that this difference was the result of decreased tracer penetration in the hypothalamus and areas of the basal forebrain (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by regional analysis data from the UNC group shown in Figure 4.

claim: CSF tracer entry along the ventral and lateral cortex was highest in the WT compared to the Aqp4+/+ control.
source: Interestingly, CSF tracer entry along the ventral and lateral cortex was highest in the WT compared to the Aqp4+/+ control (Figure 4f) suggesting possible strain-dependent differences.
evidence: This is an observation from the UNC experiments shown in Figure 4f with an interpretation.

claim: In vivo transcranial optical imaging of BSA-647 showed more CSF influx in the WT compared to the KO.
source: In vivo transcranial optical imaging (Plog et al., 2018) of the far-red BSA-647 showed more CSF influx in the WT compared to the KO (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo imaging data from the URMC group shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tracer evidently entered the brain parenchyma through a network of perivascular spaces of the large cerebral arteries on the pial surface.
source: Tracer evidently entered the brain parenchyma through a network of perivascular spaces of the large cerebral arteries on the pial surface.
evidence: This is an observation from the URMC in vivo imaging experiments.

claim: More tracer could be found on the dorsal cortical surface of WT mice compared to Aqp4 KO mice.
source: More tracer could be found on the dorsal cortical surface of WT mice compared to Aqp4 KO mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the URMC in vivo imaging experiments.

claim: The KO mice had less influx for both the 3 kDa dextran and the 66 kDa BSA compared to the WT (~32.7% and ~47.06%, respectively).
source: The KO mice had less influx for both the 3 kDa dextran and the 66 kDa BSA compared to the WT (~32.7% and ~47.06%, respectively), despite the 22x difference in molecular weight (Figure 5c–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the URMC group shown in Figure 5.

claim: Aqp4 deletion reduced CSF entry through the glymphatic pathway by ~42.4% in a replicate experiment with half the injection volume and rate.
source: In a replicate experiment where the injection volume and injection rate was half of the previous, Aqp4 deletion also reduced CSF entry through the glymphatic pathway by ~42.4% (Figure 5f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a replicate URMC experiment shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tracer penetration into brain was found to be ~2 fold higher in the WT than in the KO mice.
source: Tracer penetration into brain was found to be ~2 fold higher in the WT than in the KO mice (Figure 5i).
evidence: This claim is supported by tracer depth analysis from the URMC group shown in Figure 5.

claim: Snta1 KO mice lack expression of the adaptor protein α-syntrophin.
source: To assess the role of perivascular astrocytic localization of AQP4 in mediating CSF flux into the brain parenchyma, we utilized the Snta1 KO mouse line. These mice lack expression of the adaptor protein α-syntrophin, which links AQP4 to the dystrophin associated complex and is critical for maintenance of the perivascular localization of AQP4 (Jessen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a characterization of the Snta1 KO mouse line supported by citation.

claim: α-syntrophin links AQP4 to the dystrophin associated complex and is critical for maintenance of the perivascular localization of AQP4.
source: These mice lack expression of the adaptor protein α-syntrophin, which links AQP4 to the dystrophin associated complex and is critical for maintenance of the perivascular localization of AQP4 (Jessen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic claim about α-syntrophin function supported by citation.

claim: Immunolabeling of AQP4 illustrates the loss of AQP4 perivascular localization in the Snta1 KO mice.
source: Immunolabeling of AQP4 illustrates the loss of AQP4 perivascular localization in the Snta1 KO mice (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data from the OHSU group shown in Figure 6.

claim: While perivascular localization is lost in Snta1 KO mice, widespread AQP4 expression is still detectable by immunofluorescence.
source: Higher magnification imaging reveals that, while perivascular localization is lost, widespread AQP4 expression is still detectable by immunofluorescence, consistent with a previous characterization of the mouse line (Figure 6a–b insets (Neely et al., 2001)).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from the OHSU group shown in Figure 6 and a citation.

claim: At 30 min after the start of the injection, elevated levels of Gad were detected in both WT mice and Snta1 KO mice, particularly along the ventral surface of the brain.
source: At 30 min after the start of the injection, elevated levels of Gad were detected in both WT mice and Snta1 KO mice, particularly along the ventral surface of the brain (Figure 6e–f), but by 60 min Gad signal within the parenchyma of Snta1 KO mice was significantly reduced compared to wild type mice (Figure 6g,h,n).
evidence: This claim is supported by DCE-MRI data from the OHSU group shown in Figure 6.

claim: By 60 min Gad signal within the parenchyma of Snta1 KO mice was significantly reduced compared to wild type mice.
source: At 30 min after the start of the injection, elevated levels of Gad were detected in both WT mice and Snta1 KO mice, particularly along the ventral surface of the brain (Figure 6e–f), but by 60 min Gad signal within the parenchyma of Snta1 KO mice was significantly reduced compared to wild type mice (Figure 6g,h,n).
evidence: This claim is supported by DCE-MRI data from the OHSU group shown in Figure 6.

claim: Regional assessment revealed decreased signal in Snta1 KO mice across brain regions, which was most pronounced in cortex and hippocampus compared to subcortical brain regions and within the ventricles.
source: Regional assessment revealed decreased signal in Snta1 KO mice across brain regions, which was most pronounced in cortex and hippocampus compared to subcortical brain regions and within the ventricles (Figure 6j–m).
evidence: This claim is supported by regional analysis of DCE-MRI data from the OHSU group shown in Figure 6.

claim: The perivascular localization of AQP4 contributes to the kinetics of CSF influx into the brain parenchyma.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that the perivascular localization of AQP4 contributes to the kinetics of CSF influx into the brain parenchyma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Snta1 KO results from the OHSU group.

claim: The two groups exposed to invasive surgery exhibited markedly suppressed CSF tracer influx compared with the control group.
source: The analysis showed that the two groups exposed to invasive surgery exhibited markedly suppressed CSF tracer influx compared with the control group (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the URMC group shown in Figure 7.

claim: The suppression of CSF tracer influx in animals with insertion of the glass pipettes was symmetric with no difference in tracer influx between the ipsilateral and the contralateral hemisphere.
source: The suppression of CSF tracer influx in animals with insertion of the glass pipettes was symmetric with no difference in tracer influx between the ipsilateral and the contralateral hemisphere (p > 0.05, 3–5 slices per animal, n = 7, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the URMC data.

claim: Invasive procedures acutely suppress brain-wide CSF influx.
source: These observations show that invasive procedures acutely suppresses brain-wide CSF influx and that tracer injection should not be used in the study of the glymphatic system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Results from the overall meta-analysis showed a significant decrease in the transport of the injected substance in Aqp4 KO mice relative to controls (SMD: −1.88 [-2.88; −0.87]; p = 0.0003).
source: Results from the overall meta-analysis showed a significant decrease in the transport of the injected substance in Aqp4 KO mice relative to controls (−1.88 [-2.88; −0.87]; p = 0.0003) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 70.0%, p = 0.0008; Figure 8b).
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analysis results shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The meta-analysis for CSF influx studies demonstrated a significant overall decrease in tracer entry in Aqp4 KO mice compared to controls (SMD: −1.70 [−2.49; −0.90]; p<0.0001).
source: Standardized mean differences (SMD) were used in the meta-analysis to account for different outcome measures (e.g. fluorescence intensity, thresholded area, % injected radiation), and demonstrated a significant overall decrease in tracer entry in Aqp4 KO mice compared to controls (SMD with 95% confidence interval: −1.70 [−2.49; −0.90]; p<0.0001) with a high degree of interstudy heterogeneity (I2 = 73.1%; p<0.0001; Figure 8a).
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analysis results shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The high degree of heterogeneity in the CSF influx meta-analysis was primarily caused by three datasets extracted from Smith et al.
source: As expected based on the direction and magnitude of the effect estimates reported in the studies, the high degree of heterogeneity was primarily caused by three datasets extracted from Smith et al.
evidence: This is an interpretation from the meta-analysis sensitivity analysis.

claim: The KO line used, the age of the mice, the anesthetic protocol, and the injection rate explained a significant proportion of the observed variance between the datasets in the CSF influx meta-analysis.
source: The KO line used (p = 0.0001, Test of Moderators), the age of the mice (p = 0.0006), the anesthetic protocol (p < 0.0001), and the injection rate (p < 0.0001) explained a significant proportion of the observed variance between the datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-regression analysis results.

claim: The variables that explained the largest proportion of heterogeneity in the CSF influx meta-analysis were anesthesia type and injection rate.
source: The variables that explained the largest proportion of heterogeneity were anesthesia type and injection rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the meta-regression analysis.

claim: Animal age was a significant source of heterogeneity, accounting for 85.28% of the variance between studies in the CSF influx meta-analysis.
source: Animal age was also a significant source of heterogeneity, accounting for 85.28% of the variance between studies.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-regression analysis.

claim: Both anesthesia and aging have been shown to modify the degree of intracisternal tracer entry.
source: Although it is not possible to determine the exact role that these covariates played in the observed results, both anesthesia and aging have been shown to modify the degree of intracisternal tracer entry, providing another potential explanation for the observed heterogeneity (Benveniste et al., 2017; Kress et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two independent single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) variant association studies identified multiple SNPs in the Aqp4 gene that were associated with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and increased Aβ burden in humans with reduced sleep quality.
source: Supporting evidence of this has also been shown in humans; two independent single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) variant association studies identified multiple SNPs in the Aqp4 gene that were associated with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and increased Aβ burden in humans with reduced sleep quality (Burfeind, 2017; AIBL Research Group et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human genetic studies.

claim: Reduced perivascular polarization of AQP4 was a significant predictor of AD status in postmortem human brains.
source: A separate study by the OHSU group also found that reduced perivascular polarization of AQP4 was a significant predictor of AD status in postmortem human brains (Zeppenfeld et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human postmortem study.

claim: Deletion of astrocytic water channels suppressed both the influx of CSF tracers injected into the cisterna magna and the efflux of tracers infused directly into striatum.
source: The original report from the URMC group on the glymphatic system showed that deletion of astrocytic water channels suppressed both the influx of CSF tracers injected into the cisterna magna and the efflux of tracers infused directly into striatum (Iliff et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Aβ accumulation and cerebral amyloid angiopathy were significantly increased in a double-hit murine model with Aqp4 deletion and Aβ over-expression.
source: Follow-up of that finding by the NMU group documented that Aβ accumulation and cerebral amyloid angiopathy were significantly increased in a double-hit murine model with Aqp4 deletion and Aβ over-expression (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Deletion of Aqp4 significantly reduced clearance of AAV.
source: The UNC group showed that deletion of Aqp4 significantly reduced clearance of AAV (Murlidharan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Smith et al. (2017) failed to meet requirements for a proper replication study in several key respects.
source: However, Smith et al. (2017) failed to meet these requirements in several key respects.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the Smith et al. study methodology.

claim: Iliff et al. used ketamine/xylazine (KX) anesthesia rather than tribromoethanol (Avertin).
source: In particular, Iliff et al. used ketamine/xylazine (KX) anesthesia rather than tribromoethanol (Avertin) (Iliff et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological comparison between studies.

claim: Xylazine is an α2 adrenergic agonist that blocks release of norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus projections across the neuraxis.
source: Xylazine is an α2 adrenergic agonist that blocks release of norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus projections across the neuraxis.
evidence: This is a pharmacological description of xylazine.

claim: Norepinephrine has been identified as the key humoral regulator of glymphatic solute transport.
source: This is an important point, because norepinephrine has been identified as the key humoral regulator of glymphatic solute transport (Xie et al., 2013), and norepinephrine attenuates glymphatic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Norepinephrine attenuates glymphatic function.
source: This is an important point, because norepinephrine has been identified as the key humoral regulator of glymphatic solute transport (Xie et al., 2013), and norepinephrine attenuates glymphatic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and established knowledge.

claim: Avertin is not approved for use in several European countries and is restricted to terminal procedures in the US.
source: Avertin is not approved for use in several European countries and is restricted to terminal procedures in the US (Arras et al., 2001; Meyer and Fish, 2005).
evidence: This claim about regulatory status is supported by citations.

claim: Groothuis et al. (2007) reported that parenchymal solute efflux was 100-fold slower in rats anesthetized with pentobarbital than those that received ketamine/xylazine.
source: The importance of the anesthetic agent in the present context was first highlighted by Groothuis et al. (2007), who reported that parenchymal solute efflux was 100-fold slower in rats anesthetized with pentobarbital than those that received ketamine/xylazine.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Benveniste et al. reported a marked difference in influx of contrast agents in isoflurane-anesthetized animals versus low-dose isoflurane plus dexmedetomidine.
source: Anesthesia-dependent effects were also noted by Benveniste et al., that reported a marked difference in influx of contrast agents in isoflurane-anesthetized animals versus low-dose isoflurane plus dexmedetomidine (an α2 agonist) (Benveniste et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: The UNC group used ketamine/xylazine anesthesia and observed AQP4-dependent glymphatic transport despite using the same Aqp4 KO mouse line as Smith et al. (2017).
source: The importance of anesthesia is supported by the experiments reported here: The UNC group used ketamine/xylazine anesthesia and observed AQP4-dependent glymphatic transport (Figure 4), despite using the same Aqp4 KO mouse line as in the Smith et al. (2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the UNC group.

claim: Smith et al. did not provide key methodological details such as the injection approach and rate, anesthesia, or the age of the animals for data collected in rats.
source: In addition, the methodology of Smith et al. was not presented in sufficient detail to assess the fidelity of the replication. Key methodological details, such as the injection approach and rate,anesthesia, or the age of the animals were not provided for data collected in rats.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the Smith et al. methodology.

claim: Smith et al. did not assess whether Aqp4 was deleted in CNS of the rats used in their study.
source: Neither did the investigators assess whether Aqp4 was deleted in CNS albeit this was the first report utilizing Aqp4 KO rats.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the Smith et al. methodology.

claim: Increasing anesthesia concentration decreased glymphatic function.
source: A recent study reported that increasing anesthesia concentration decreased glymphatic function (Gakuba et al., 2018), as opposed to the original finding that the glymphatic system is maximally active during natural sleep or anesthesia (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: The glymphatic system is maximally active during natural sleep or anesthesia.
source: A recent study reported that increasing anesthesia concentration decreased glymphatic function (Gakuba et al., 2018), as opposed to the original finding that the glymphatic system is maximally active during natural sleep or anesthesia (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Awakening from general anesthesia is associated with cognitive disturbances.
source: This is not a valid approach, because awakening from general anesthesia is associated with cognitive disturbances (Su et al., 2016; Paredes et al., 2016; Numan et al., 2017) and inhaled anesthetics in particular are linked to a high rate of delirium upon emergence from anesthesia (Brioni et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

source: In our experience, experimenter error during cisterna magna injections is a significant source of variability (Xavier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation based on experience and supported by citation.

claim: Interstitial tracers are cleared from brain tissue at rates that are independent of molecular weight.
source: The initial study articulating the glymphatic model confirmed seminal work by Cserr and colleagues that interstitial tracers are cleared from brain tissue at rates that are independent of molecular weight (Iliff et al., 2012; Cserr et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies.

claim: A large body of indirect experimental evidence supports the occurrence of bulk flow in the periarterial space in the brain.
source: A large body of indirect experimental evidence supports the occurrence of bulk flow in the periarterial space in the brain (see reviews by Hladky and Barrand, 2014 and Nicholson and Hrabětová, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Smith et al. (2017) stated that 'occasionally, when the injected dextran entered the perivascular space of vessels near the injection site, both large and small dextrans traveled substantial distances away from the injection site'.
source: Smith et al. (2017) themselves provide such evidence, stating that 'occasionally, when the injected dextran entered the perivascular space of vessels near the injection site, both large and small dextrans traveled substantial distances away from the injection site' (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct quote from the Smith et al. study.

claim: Perivascular flow is peristaltic, propelled by pulsations of the arterial walls.
source: There is also indirect evidence that this flow is peristaltic, propelled by pulsations of the arterial walls (e.g. Hadaczek et al. (2006)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Mestre et al. showed that perivascular flow pulses in synchrony with the heartbeat, is driven by pulsations of the arterial wall, and produces a net flow in the same direction as the blood flow.
source: Using two-photon microscopy and particle-tracking velocimetry, Mestre et al. gathered hundreds of thousands of velocity measurements at sampling rates up to 30 Hz over half hour experiments, mapping the perivascular flow in space and time in great detail: their results show that the flow pulses in synchrony with the heartbeat, is driven by pulsations of the arterial wall, and produces a net (average) flow in the same direction as the blood flow.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from a cited study (Mestre et al., 2018).

claim: As a consequence of bulk flow along periarterial spaces, there must be an outlet for this directional flow: conservation of mass demands that this volumetric flow must continue through other parts of the glymphatic system.
source: As a consequence of the now well-established bulk flow along periarterial spaces, there must be an outlet for this directional flow: conservation of mass - as expressed by the continuity equation - demands that this volumetric flow must continue through other parts of the glymphatic system – that is, in the neuropil and the perivenous spaces.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on physical principles.

claim: Flow speeds will be lower in the neuropil because of the much larger total cross-sectional area of the available extracellular flow channels, and due to the availability of the gap junction-coupled astroglial syncytium as an intracellular route for water and solute movement.
source: Although the full volumetric net flow must pass through the neuropil, flow speeds will be lower there because of the much larger total cross-sectional area of the available extracellular flow channels, and due to the availability of the gap junction-coupled astroglial syncytium as an intracellular route for water and solute movement (Asgari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by citation.

claim: A meta-analysis that included more than 200 Aqp4 KO mice and rats studied so far added further support to the finding that glymphatic influx and efflux are both highly dependent upon AQP4 expression.
source: In fact, a meta-analysis that include the more than 200 Aqp4 KO mice and rats studied so far added further support to the finding that glymphatic influx and efflux are both highly dependent upon AQP4 expression (Figure 8 , Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results presented in Figure 8.

claim: The meta-analysis identified the anesthesia protocol, wide age range of the experimental animals and the injection paradigm as potential causes for the conflicting data reported by Smith et al.
source: The meta-analysis identified the anesthesia protocol, wide age range of the experimental animals and the injection paradigm are potential causes for the conflicting data reported by Smith et al.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the meta-analysis.

claim: Glymphatic transport is affected by the sleep-wake cycle.
source: However, it is important to note that glymphatic transport is affected by multiple pathways other than AQP4. For example, the sleep-wake cycle (Xie et al., 2013), brain injury in the setting of trauma or ischemia (Iliff et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017), exercise (He et al., 2017; von Holstein-Rathlou et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2018), amyloid-β accumulation and acute amyloid-β toxicity (Xu et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2016), omega-3 fatty acids (Ren et al., 2017), plasma osmolarity (Plog et al., 2018), and aging (Kress et al., 2014) are important regulators of glymphatic transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: The primary role of AQP channels is to lower the driving forces for fluid transport across the plasma membranes.
source: The primary role of AQP channels is to lower the driving forces for fluid transport across the plasma membranes (Verkman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: AQP4 is highly enriched in astrocytic endfeet facing the perivascular space.
source: AQP4 is highly enriched in astrocytic endfeet facing the perivascular space and thus strategically positioned to facilitate CSF exchange with interstitial fluid.
evidence: This is an anatomical description supported by established knowledge.

claim: Loss of the polarized expression of AQP4 in reactive astrocytes leads to a reduction in parenchymal CSF tracer influx.
source: Accordingly, loss of the polarized expression of AQP4 in reactive astrocytes lead to a reduction in parenchymal CSF tracer influx (Iliff et al., 2014; Kress et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of AQP4 potentiated the increases in intracranial pressure in a murine model of hydrocephalus.
source: Moreover, deletion of AQP4 potentiated the increases in intracranial pressure in a murine model of hydrocephalus consistent with the notion that AQP4 supports and facilitates intraparenchymal fluid flow (Bloch et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Smith and Verkman (2018) claim that solute transport in the parenchyma is primarily driven by diffusion rather than convection (bulk flow).
source: The claim by Smith and Verkman (2018) that solute transport in the parenchyma is primarily driven by diffusion rather than convection (bulk flow) is based on their finding of a dependence of this transport on the size of the solute particles.
evidence: This summarizes a claim from Smith and Verkman (2018).

claim: Smith and Verkman claim that diffusive transport depends strongly on particle size, whereas convective transport does not, so long as the ratio of the particle size to the pore or channel size is less than about 0.5.
source: They claim that diffusive transport depends strongly on particle size, whereas convective transport does not, so long as the ratio of the particle size to the pore or channel size is less than about 0.5.
evidence: This summarizes a claim from Smith and Verkman.

claim: The reference cited by Smith and Verkman (Dechadilok and Deen, 2009) does not support their claim, but instead shows a significant dependence of flow resistance on particle size for much smaller particles.
source: In support of this claim, they cite a single reference (Dechadilok and Deen, 2009), which does not actually support their claim, but instead shows a significant dependence of flow resistance on particle size for much smaller particles.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the citation used by Smith and Verkman.

claim: Recent modeling studies suggest that at the smallest microscopic scales, encompassing small numbers of vessels and the interposed neuropil, diffusion is sufficient to account for observed solute movement.
source: Their findings are in general agreement with recent modeling studies suggesting that at the smallest microscopic scales, encompassing small numbers of vessels and the interposed neuropil, diffusion is sufficient to account for observed solute movement (Asgari et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2016; Holter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: These modeling findings do not exclude a contribution of bulk flow within the entire interstitium.
source: However, it is important to note that these findings do not exclude a contribution of bulk flow within the entire interstitium, and do not determine whether the experimental approaches used to detect flow on the microscopic scale are sufficiently sensitive to detect bulk flow occurring at very low flow rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation and critique of the modeling studies.

claim: The majority of the studies contradicting the glymphatic model are based on theoretical modeling and not experimental evidence.
source: Also, the majority of the studies contradicting the glymphatic model are based on theoretical modeling and not experimental evidence (Asgari et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2016; Faghih and Sharp, 2018).
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by citations.

claim: There is a need to develop more appropriate technical approaches for evaluating slow interstitial bulk flow over long distances.
source: Thus, as articulated by Holter et al. in their recent modeling study (Holter et al., 2017), there is a need to develop more appropriate technical approaches for evaluating slow interstitial bulk flow over long distances (Ratner et al., 2017), such as DCE-MRI in nonhuman primates or human subjects.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the limitations of current methods, supported by citations.
